title: The Operating Model Advantage: Why AI Winners Are Rewiring Their Organizations
author: Christoph Schmitz · Dago Diedrich · Gianmarco Cilento · Steffen Fuchs

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that AI value depends on selective task allocation and operating-model redesign rather than simply adding tools to existing work. It materially extends that proposition with an enterprise transformation sequence—decompose workflows, allocate tasks between AI and humans, redesign talent and governance, then select technology—and survey evidence associating workflow redesign with stronger EBIT impact, while treating that evidence as correlational.
qs: That process starts by decomposing existing workflows into discrete tasks and determining which activities should shift to AI and which should remain under human control.
Most organizations—roughly 79 percent—skip this step, yet McKinsey research identifies workflow redesign as the factor most strongly correlated with enterprise EBIT impact.

st.t: Work redesign: Organisation captures more value than access
st.an: The source directly endorses the cluster’s central proposition that durable AI value depends more on redesigning workflows, coordination, governance and talent than on tool access alone. It also supports the synthesis’s qualification that redesign is an enabling capability rather than value in itself, while its survey results and company cases are associations and illustrations rather than proof of universal returns.
qs: Most companies are using AI to accelerate existing activities while leaving the underlying operating model, including governance, teams, and capabilities, largely unchanged.

Rewiring the organization is not the source of value by itself; it is the mechanism that allows companies to create new products, strengthen customer relationships, build proprietary data assets, and capture emerging profit pools as AI reshapes competition.

kp.k: Organizational redesign, not tool access, differentiates AI outcomes
kp.d: In this cross-industry article, the authors argue that widespread AI deployment has produced limited enterprise-wide financial benefits because companies accelerate existing activities without changing governance, teams, capabilities or approval structures. They predict that increasingly accessible technology will make organizational operating models, rather than the tools themselves, the basis of competitive advantage.
qs: Most companies are using AI to accelerate existing activities while leaving the underlying operating model, including governance, teams, and capabilities, largely unchanged.

Companies using similar technologies are already producing very different outcomes, suggesting that competitive advantage is moving away from the tools themselves and toward the organizations that deploy them.

kp.k: Efficiency alone is unlikely to create durable advantage
kp.d: The authors distinguish productivity improvements, which they expect to become standard as AI diffuses, from organizational redesign that enables innovation, new offerings and access to emerging profit pools. They argue that operating models are difficult to copy because they emerge from accumulated choices about workflows, governance, talent, data and decisions.
qs: In fact, many efficiency gains are likely to become table stakes as AI diffuses.

Unlike software or infrastructure, operating models cannot simply be purchased or replicated overnight; they develop through accumulated organizational choices about workflows, governance, people and talent, data, and decision-making.

kp.k: Infrastructure investment makes AI increasingly accessible
kp.d: The article estimates that hyperscalers invested $1.3 trillion to $1.6 trillion in AI-related capital expenditures since 2023, with roughly three-quarters going to AI-specific infrastructure, and that AI tools reach 1.0 billion to 1.5 billion users globally. The authors use these estimates to frame AI as a mainstream business tool rather than a scarce frontier technology.
qs: Since 2023, hyperscalers have invested an estimated $1.3 trillion to $1.6 trillion in AI-related capital expenditures, with roughly three-quarters directed toward AI-specific infrastructure.
AI tools now reach an estimated 1.0 billion to 1.5 billion users globally.

kp.k: Railways illustrate value capture through new business models
kp.d: Drawing an analogy with the American railway boom of the 1860s through the 1890s, the authors argue that the greatest gains accrued to businesses reorganizing around newly possible activities, rather than simply shipping faster or building infrastructure. They cite Sears catalog sales, estimated to command 1 percent of the US economy at their peak, and Swift's reorganization of meatpacking around refrigerated railcars.
qs: Instead, the biggest winners were those that created entirely new operating models, reshaped industry economics, and captured value pools that could not have existed without rail.
The US meat company Swift reorganized meatpacking around refrigerated railcars, reshaping an entire industry in the process.

kp.k: Reported survey links redesign with stronger AI returns
kp.d: The article reports a McKinsey survey finding that only 21 percent of companies fundamentally redesigned operating models around AI. Top performers, defined as attributing 5 percent or more of EBIT to AI, were three times more likely to pursue broad operating-model redesign and twice as likely to redesign workflows before selecting tools. These are reported associations; the article supplies no sample size.
qs: This problem is widespread, with a recent McKinsey survey finding that only 21 percent of companies had fundamentally redesigned their operating models around AI.

In fact, the McKinsey survey showed that top performers—companies attributing 5 percent or more of EBIT to AI—were three times more likely to pursue broad operating model redesign and twice as likely to redesign workflows before selecting AI tools.

kp.k: Macroeconomic improvement is linked to AI power users
kp.d: The article reports approximately 2.7 percent US productivity growth in 2025, against a 1.4 percent average over the previous decade, alongside fewer than 200,000 additional jobs and 3.7 percent GDP growth. It presents these figures as supporting the view that some companies benefit from AI and reports a separate analysis attributing much of the improvement to a small cohort redesigning workflows around AI.
qs: US productivity growth accelerated to approximately 2.7 percent in 2025—nearly double the 1.4 percent average of the previous decade—even as the economy added fewer than 200,000 jobs and GDP grew 3.7 percent.
According to one analysis, a relatively small cohort of AI power users is driving much of this improvement by redesigning workflows around AI.

kp.k: Growing coordination costs constrain large enterprises
kp.d: The authors describe a 'complexity scissors' mechanism: revenue growth slows as markets mature while review boards, management layers and cross-functional coordination continue becoming more costly. They illustrate potential communication links rising from ten in a five-person team to 1,225 in a 50-person team and report McKinsey research that fewer than one in ten large companies sustain above-cost-of-capital returns over a decade.
qs: A five-person team has only ten communication links; a 50-person team has 1,225.
But coordination costs, including those for review boards, management layers, and cross-functional committees, continue to rise.
Fewer than one in ten large companies sustain above-cost-of-capital returns over a decade.

kp.k: AI could replace coordination layers and management tasks
kp.d: The authors propose centralized AI orchestration and hub-and-spoke structures as alternatives to extensive bilateral coordination. They argue that AI can synthesize information, prioritize actions, forecast outcomes and coordinate work, with some management and decision responsibilities delegated to agents. Their assertions that this can accelerate decisions and eliminate potential bias describe proposed capabilities and benefits, rather than quantified results.
qs: Rather than relying on growing numbers of person-to-person interactions, AI systems can route information, decisions, and workflows through centralized orchestration layers based on clear, nonpolitical, ROIC-oriented factors or governance criteria.
In many cases, companies can delegate decision-making responsibilities and other management tasks to AI agents.
AI is different because it targets the coordination layer itself.

kp.k: Bolt-on adoption preserves bottlenecks and can propagate errors
kp.d: The authors identify three failure mechanisms: unchanged complexity and roles, task-level gains trapped by broader workflow bottlenecks, and success metrics focused on deployments rather than outcomes. They report McKinsey research warning that agents in workflows not redesigned for them can propagate errors at machine speed. They recommend decision-cycle speed, coordination costs, financial performance and ROIC over license or pilot counts.
qs: McKinsey research shows that when agentic systems operate inside workflows that were not redesigned for them, errors can propagate across the organization at machine speed.
Individual activities become faster, but broader workflows do not.

They often gauge success by the number of AI-related licenses, pilots, and deployments, rather than by business outcomes such as faster decision cycles, lower coordination costs, or improved financial performance.

kp.k: Workforce capability building precedes documented industrial gains
kp.d: The article presents Emirates Global Aluminium as an example of people and process transformation preceding AI deployment: thousands of employees trained through a digital academy before AI was deployed across smelting operations. It reports more than $120 million in documented impact after a multiyear effort, including 170 percent ROI and double-digit throughput and labor-productivity improvements.
qs: Emirates Global Aluminium, for example, first trained thousands of employees through a dedicated digital academy before deploying AI across smelting operations.
After a multiyear effort, the company ultimately documented more than $120 million in impact, including a 170 percent ROI and double-digit improvements in throughput and labor productivity.

kp.k: Freeport increased production by accelerating operational decisions
kp.d: The Freeport-McMoRan case contrasts a new concentrator costing $1.5 billion to $2 billion and requiring eight to ten years with extracting more output from existing assets. Cross-functional teams developed machine learning using second-by-second sensor data and centralized cloud architecture. At Bagdad, changing settings hourly instead of once per shift reportedly increased copper production 10 percent within months while also improving recovery rates.
qs: Building a new concentrator—a processing plant that separates copper minerals from waste rock—would cost $1.5 billion to $2 billion and take eight to ten years through permitting and construction.
The company then began adjusting settings hourly rather than once per shift.
Within months, copper production at Bagdad increased 10 percent, and recovery rates improved—a dual achievement that metallurgists describe as “elusive” at mature assets.

kp.k: Reusable architecture supports scaling, with portfolio benefits projected
kp.d: The article reports that about 60 percent of Bagdad's code was directly reusable across all seven concentrator sites in the Americas, with successive deployments becoming faster through existing capabilities, architecture and agile methods. It distinguishes these deployment observations from projected portfolio impact: output comparable to opening a new mine and hundreds of millions in EBITDA improvement without a new facility's capital cycles, permitting and environmental issues.
qs: From the outset, Freeport-McMoRan built AI models with modular architecture, and about 60 percent of the code developed at Bagdad was directly reusable across all seven concentrator sites in the Americas.
The projected impact across the portfolio was similar to that resulting from opening a new mine and included hundreds of millions in projected EBITDA improvement.

kp.k: Accumulated transformation knowledge creates a capability moat
kp.d: The authors distinguish a capability moat from a strategic moat: accumulated experience redesigning workflows, governing AI decisions, deploying talent and managing change enables companies to build multiple competitive advantages. They argue that this learning makes subsequent transformations faster, cheaper and more likely to succeed, supporting proprietary data flywheels, embedded customer workflows and new business models.
qs: The result is not a strategic moat in itself but a capability moat—an organizational strength that enables companies to build and scale multiple strategic moats.
Competitors can deploy similar AI tools, but they cannot easily replicate years of organizational learning, experimentation, workflow redesign, and operating experience.

kp.k: Concentrate investment in economically significant business domains
kp.d: The authors recommend concentrating AI investment in one to three high-value domains rather than spreading it thinly. Selection criteria are economic potential, proprietary data that become more valuable with use, and workflow complexity. They report that, in a McKinsey analysis of leading transformations, companies targeting EBITDA improvements of 20 percent or more in priority domains achieved roughly $3 incremental EBITDA per dollar invested, breaking even within one to two years.
qs: McKinsey research suggests that winners concentrate AI investment in one to three high-value business domains.

Companies that sought to improve EBITDA by 20 percent or more in priority domains achieved roughly $3 in incremental EBITDA for every dollar invested, with breakeven occurring within one to two years.

kp.k: Business leaders should own transformation before technology selection
kp.d: The authors recommend business and P&L leaders, rather than IT functions, as primary decision-makers because transformation should pursue competitive advantage and resource allocation rather than tool optimization. They report McKinsey research placing failure rates above 80 percent for transformations led primarily as technology programs and attribute this to insufficient operational redesign.
qs: The central question is where the company can create competitive advantage, and that means business and P&L (profit-and-loss) leaders—not IT functions—should be the primary decision-makers.

McKinsey research suggests that AI transformations led primarily as technology programs fail at significantly higher rates—more than 80 percent—because they optimize tools rather than changing how companies work by redesigning operations.

kp.k: Redesign workflows, then talent, then select technology
kp.d: The recommended sequence begins with decomposing workflows into tasks and determining which shift to AI and which remain under human control. The authors state that roughly 79 percent of organizations skip this step and report workflow redesign as the factor most strongly correlated with enterprise EBIT impact. They place supporting talent-model development before technology selection.
qs: That process starts by decomposing existing workflows into discrete tasks and determining which activities should shift to AI and which should remain under human control.
Most organizations—roughly 79 percent—skip this step, yet McKinsey research identifies workflow redesign as the factor most strongly correlated with enterprise EBIT impact.
Redesign workflows first, build the supporting talent model second, and select technology third.

kp.k: Toyota reportedly reduced planning staffing through redeployment
kp.d: The article describes Toyota replacing a global resource-allocation process involving spreadsheets, large planning teams, multiple approvals and weeks of effort with an AI-mediated workflow that processes demand and supply constraints and guides planners through scenarios in minutes. It reports a planning-team reduction exceeding 80 percent through redeployment into higher-value critical-thinking work, explicitly not layoffs.
qs: Toyota replaced that process with an AI-mediated workflow that pulls demand data, evaluates supply constraints, and walks planners through scenarios in minutes.

The planning team shrank by more than 80 percent—not through layoffs, but through redeployment into higher-value work that required critical thinking—while coordination layers between data and decisions compressed dramatically.

kp.k: Dual operating models enable transformation alongside ongoing business
kp.d: McKinsey's recommended dual operating model maintains core operations while establishing agile pods in selected domains with different decision rights, performance metrics and talent models. The authors suggest early wins within 12 to 18 months can build support, generate proprietary data and finance expansion. The Rewired framework also emphasizes a value-focused road map, expert talent, speed-enabling organization, distributed technology, embedded data and adoption at scale.
qs: While the core business continues operating largely as before, companies establish agile pods within selected transformation domains.
These pods often operate with different decision rights, performance metrics, and talent models than the broader organization.
Early wins within the first 12 to 18 months can generate confidence, create proprietary operational data, and help fund broader deployment efforts.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Schmitz, Diedrich, Cilento and Fuchs argue that enterprise AI advantage increasingly depends on organizational redesign rather than access to technology.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain corporate operating-model article, not a source about legal services. The authors claim that widespread deployment has so far produced limited enterprise-wide financial benefits because companies accelerate tasks without changing governance, teams, capabilities or decision processes. As AI tools become widely accessible, they predict that efficiency improvements will become table stakes, while organizational capabilities will enable more durable differentiation through innovation, new offerings, proprietary data and emerging profit pools.

pts.k: The authors claim that AI can change the economics of enterprise coordination, including delegating some management decisions to agents.
pts.d: They describe a shift from numerous person-to-person interactions to centralized AI orchestration that routes information and workflows according to governance and ROIC criteria. They claim this can reduce meetings, management layers and decision delays, and distinguish it from earlier transformations that largely preserved coordination structures. This goes beyond adding a copilot to existing tasks: some decision-making and management responsibilities could shift to AI, although their recommended workflow analysis explicitly retains some activities under human control.

pts.k: The authors argue that bolt-on AI traps value at task level and can propagate errors, while focused workflow transformation produces larger business gains.
pts.d: They identify unchanged complexity, static team composition, workflow bottlenecks and deployment-based rather than outcome-based metrics as reasons for limited returns. They recommend concentrating investment in one to three high-value domains, redesigning workflows before talent models and technology selection, and placing business and P&L leaders in charge. Their claim about machine-speed error propagation concerns agentic systems in unsuitable workflows, not measured hallucination rates. They also argue that repeat transformations become faster and cheaper as organizational knowledge accumulates.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors support their operating-model argument primarily with McKinsey surveys and transformation research, reporting associations and financial outcomes.
pts.d: The article reports that only 21 percent of companies fundamentally redesigned operating models around AI. Companies attributing at least 5 percent of EBIT to AI were reportedly three times as likely to pursue broad operating-model redesign and twice as likely to redesign workflows before choosing tools. It separately states that roughly 79 percent skip task-level workflow decomposition and that workflow redesign is the factor most strongly correlated with enterprise EBIT impact. A McKinsey analysis of leading transformations reportedly found roughly $3 in incremental EBITDA per dollar invested among companies targeting improvements of at least 20 percent in priority domains. The authors also report failure rates exceeding 80 percent for transformations led primarily as technology programs. These are presented as survey findings and research-based claims; the supplied text does not provide sample sizes or detailed methodologies.

pts.k: Industrial and planning case studies illustrate reported operational gains, with realized results distinguished from portfolio projections.
pts.d: The authors report that Emirates Global Aluminium trained thousands of employees before AI deployment and documented more than $120 million in impact, 170 percent ROI and double-digit throughput and labor-productivity improvements after a multiyear effort. At Freeport-McMoRan, cross-functional teams, sensor-based machine learning and hourly rather than once-per-shift settings changes reportedly increased Bagdad copper production by 10 percent within months and improved recovery rates. About 60 percent of the code was reusable across seven concentrator sites; hundreds of millions in portfolio EBITDA improvement remained projected. Toyota's AI-mediated resource-allocation workflow reportedly reduced scenario work from weeks to minutes and shrank the planning team by more than 80 percent through redeployment, not layoffs.

pts.k: The article supplements company evidence with macroeconomic figures, adoption estimates and a railway-era analogy.
pts.d: The authors cite estimated hyperscaler AI-related capital expenditure of $1.3 trillion to $1.6 trillion since 2023 and global AI-tool use of 1.0 billion to 1.5 billion people as evidence of technological accessibility. They report approximately 2.7 percent US productivity growth in 2025, compared with a 1.4 percent prior-decade average, alongside fewer than 200,000 added jobs and 3.7 percent GDP growth. They present these figures as supporting the view that some companies benefit from AI, and relay an analysis attributing much of the improvement to workflow-redesigning AI power users. Railway-era examples of Sears and Swift supply a historical analogy for value accruing to reorganizers rather than simply infrastructure builders or early adopters. Several inline footnote titles in the supplied document do not align with the adjacent subject matter, so these bases are recorded as the article presents them rather than independently established findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article distinguishes limited benefits to date from conditional near-term returns and longer-term competitive advantage.
pts.d: Writing in 2026, the authors portray AI as already mainstream but enterprise financial gains as uneven. Their reported or proposed horizons include months for Bagdad production gains, multiple years for Emirates Global Aluminium's transformation, one to two years to breakeven in selected leading transformations, and 12 to 18 months for early wins from transformation pods. Longer-term advantage depends on accumulating organizational learning as AI diffuses; no fixed date is given for that shift. Recommended conditions include economically significant domains, proprietary data, coordination-heavy workflows, business-led decision-making, workforce capabilities and explicit allocation of tasks between AI and humans. A dual operating model is proposed to preserve ongoing operations while selected domains change.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern large enterprises, corporate leaders, managers, operational employees and competitors; no legal-sector effects are asserted.
pts.d: Large enterprises are portrayed as particularly constrained by coordination overhead. CEOs and P&L leaders are asked to lead investment and redesign decisions instead of treating AI as IT procurement. Managers may see decision-making and coordination responsibilities reassigned to AI agents. Employees need training and revised roles; Toyota illustrates redeployment into critical-thinking work rather than layoffs, not a general prediction of employment preservation. The authors identify potentially significant gains in physical-goods industries, including manufacturing, mining and distribution. Companies that build transformation capabilities may develop new offerings and stronger customer relationships, while competitors may struggle to replicate accumulated organizational experience. The article does not identify impacts on lawyers, law firms, legal buyers or access to justice.
